extracts.text:
During the 18th Century, modern methods of silkworm rearing were introduced in Karnataka during the reign of the Mysore ruler, Tipu Sultan. During the latter half of the 20th century, modern sericulture was introduced into Tamil Nadu through Hosur and Thalavadi, the border areas adjoining Karnataka.

Subsequently, the impact of the Intensive Sericulture Development Programme, the introduction of high-yielding silkworm hybrids, their higher productivity and yield, and the assurance of stable income led to the spread of sericulture to other districts of the State.

2. Heritage of Tamil Nadu’s Silk Industry

Tamil Nadu has a long and rich tradition in the silk industry. There is evidence to show that silk has been in use in the State since the Sangam period. Renowned for its high-grade mulberry silk and exceptional craftsmanship, Tamil Nadu is one of the leading silk-producing States in India.

2

The Geographical Indication (GI)-tagged Kanchipuram silk sarees, Salem bivoltine silk dhotis, the intricate temple motif workmanship of Arani and Thirubuvanam silk sarees and the rich metallic thread (zari) workmanship of Sirumugai silk sarees, together proclaim to the world the timeless cultural glory of Tamil Nadu's silk weaving tradition.

The Department of Sericulture has been taking measures to sustain this legacy by ensuring a robust and continuous supply of raw materials. By embracing modern innovations while preserving tradition, sericulture continues to remain a sustainable livelihood activity.

3. Silk Production in the State

India is the only country in the world that produces all the four well-known varieties of silk, namely Mulberry, Eri, Tasar and Muga. Further, in India, mulberry silk is predominantly produced in the States of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Maharashtra and Telangana.

3

Tamil Nadu is at the forefront in adopting the latest technologies in mulberry cultivation, silkworm rearing and silk reeling. Tamil Nadu ranks second at the national level in bivoltine silk production.

Currently, the State has 20,568 sericulture farmers cultivating mulberry in 40,012 acres as on 01.08.2026. Farmers are assured of monthly income, as one crop of silkworm can be reared within 25–27 days and the farmers can realise income by selling their produce, the cocoons.

Sericulture is practised in all districts except Chennai. Dharmapuri is the leading district in silk reeling activities.

Silkworm rearing plays a vital role in rural development by generating employment opportunities, enhancing economic empowerment of women, increasing the income of farmers and promoting allied activities.

Based on the quality assessment of silk and the prevailing average cocoon price of the state, floor price is fixed and silk lots are admitted for auction. extracts.text:
The District administration receives complaints that certain institutions are operating without obtaining approval of the Central or State Government, affiliation from the recognised University, and recognition from the Competent Statutory Council or Board. Even among the institutions that have obtained approval, certain courses are being offered without the requisite affiliation, recognition or Statutory sanction. These institutions and courses may be in Medicine, Dentistry, Nursing, Pharmacy, Allied and Healthcare, Rehabilitation Sciences, Indian’ Systems of Medicine (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani), Homeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy and Public Health.

The Institutions operating without affiliation of recognised University, approval of State or Central Government and Statutory Councils are illegal. Such institutions often mislead students into enrolling such courses at a high cost. This results in financial loss, academic uncertainty and long-term detriment to student careers, apart from posing risks to public health and safety.

Despite instructions issued by the State Government from time to time, such unauthorised institutions and institutions conducting unapproved courses are reported in different places. This Standard Operating Procedure (hereinafter referred to as “SOP”) proposes to establish a uniform and clearly defined operational framework for district-level action against both.

2. Objective:- The objective of this SOP is to adopt procedure for-

(i) identification and verification of unauthorised institutions and institutions offering unapproved courses in Medicine, Dentistry, Nursing, Pharmacy, Allied and Healthcare, Rehabilitation Sciences, Indian Systems of Medicine (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani), Homeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy and Public Health; and

(ii) taking action on the violations through legal process and safeguarding the interests of students.

3. Nodal Authority:-

The Joint Director of Health Services shall serve as the Nodal Officer at the District Level for implementation of this SOP in respect of all health related courses covered herein. The Joint Director of Health Services shall be responsible for coordination with the District

Collector, Police authorities, the competent Universities and the concerned Statutory Councils.

The Registrar, the Tamil Nadu Dr. M.G.R. Medical University, Directorate of Medical Education and Research, Directorate of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, Directorate of Indian Medicine shall share the list of approved institutions and approved course district-wise to the Joint Director of Health Services concerned, on the First April of every year and whenever new institutions are approved or modified or closed.

4. Roles and responsibilities of the Joint Director of Health Services:-

The Joint Director of Health Services shall—

(i) compile a list of all recognized institutions offering Health related courses covered under this SOP within the district, based on the inputs received from the Deans of Government Medical Colleges, Deputy Directors of Health Services, District Health Officers, officers of the Directorate of Indian Medicine and Homeopathy and other field officers; and

1. INTRODUCTION

The livestock sector has evolved into one of

the most dynamic and resilient components of

Tamil Nadu's economy. Traditionally though it

continues to be an important source of livelihood

today extends far beyond the rural economy. The

sector contributes significantly to the growth of

agriculture, food and nutritional security, value

addition, employment, entrepreneurship and the

overall economic development of the State. With

changing consumer preferences, rising demand

for quality animal products and growing

opportunities for processing and exports, livestock

has emerged as a rising sector with immense

potential for sustained growth.

One of the defining strengths of the livestock

sector is its ability to complement agriculture. It

provides a regular and dependable source of

income, enables productive utilisation of crop

residues and common grazing resources, and

helps farmers diversify their income while

reducing production risks. Since livestock rearing

requires relatively modest land resources, it is

accessible to small and marginal farmers as well

2.2.1 Key achievements

The Government of Tamil Nadu’s Policy Research partnership with JPAL-SA has provided a formal structure for many Departments to integrate the use of evaluations to address key policy questions. The Government has now a stronger culture with an active demand for data and evidence for decision-making. Notably, the Departments of Health and Family Welfare, Social Welfare and Women Empowerment and School Education have taken up multiple studies and used the research insights to understand the underlying problems better and make improvements in policy making.

For example, the findings from the baseline and first wave of the elderly panel survey have helped State Policy for Senior Citizens especially around improving the health and nutritional status

of the elderly and reforming the social security schemes targeted at the elderly.

Consistent with the findings from the elderly panel survey that specifically shows that the elderly living alone were worse off in all aspects including physical and mental health and financial status, the Government has increased its focus on the elderly living alone through various schemes such as Doorstep Goods Delivery Scheme (Veedu Thedi Porutkal Vazhangum Thittam). Findings from the completed study on understanding the impact of the ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ Scheme on the well-being of the elderly, have also been incorporated into strengthening the implementation of the scheme by the Directorate of Public Health.

In order to strengthen and institutionalise the use of evaluations and data in policy making, “Guidelines for Programme Evaluations‟ have been issued. This creates a common framework to use evaluations in policy making and a Data Analytics Unit to support advanced analysis and use of administrative data for effective decision making.

41

The Departments of Evaluation and Applied Research (DEAR) and Economics and Statistics (DoES) have adopted digital data collection platforms. This integrates new quality assurance mechanisms to improve the usability of their generated data. JPAL-SA and the Government of Tamil Nadu, in close co-ordination with key line departments, identify top policy priorities of the State Government. This is followed by co-designing interventions that can be field tested before a State-wide scale up. 3.2.4.2 Forecasting of Crop Area and Production

The scheme aims to provide advance information on season-wise area and production of certain principal crops before the final data of area under crops is settled during Jamabandhi and the final yield rates as per the Crop Cutting Experiments (CCE) become available. The advance estimates of area and production of 56 principal food and non-food crops are worked out for the State based on the Team Meetings conducted at the District/State level, and the reports are furnished to the Government.

3.2.4.3 Crop Estimation Survey on Principal Crops

To estimate the average yield per hectare and total production of principal crops, the Directorate of Economics and Statistics conducts Crop Cutting Experiments in coordination with the Agriculture Department.

Under the General Crop Estimation Survey, Crop Cutting Experiments are conducted every Fasli year for 24 food and non-food crops

123

(Paddy, Cholam, Cumbu, Ragi, Maize, Varagu, Redgram, Blackgram, Greengram, Horsegram, Samai, Cowpea, Cotton, Sugarcane, Gingelly, Groundnut, Sunflower, Thinai, Panivaragu, Kuthiraivali, Bengalgram, Castor, Soyabean and Mochai). The data is uploaded through the Digital General Crop Estimation Survey (DGCES) App of the Government of India. Based on the data uploaded through the DGCES App, estimates of average yield per hectare and total production are arrived at and submitted to the Government.

During the year 2025-2026, a total number of 9,524 Crop Cutting Experiments have been planned and are being conducted in the Districts. For the year 2026-2027, there are 9,724 Crop Cutting Experiments have been planned.

3.2.4.4 Crop Cutting Experiments for Fruits and Vegetables

A Crop Cutting Experiment (CCE) is a scientific method used to estimate the average yield of a crop. In this method, a small, randomly selected plot in a field is harvested and the produce is weighed. The result is then used to estimate crop yield per hectare for a larger area.

124

CCEs are useful for preparing crop production statistics, assessing crop losses, and determining crop insurance compensation.

Under the Fruits and Vegetables Estimation Scheme, this Directorate conducts Crop Cutting Experiments every Fasli year for 8 fruit crops viz., Banana, Mango, Jack, Guava, Grapes, Orange, Lemon and Pineapple and 5 vegetable crops viz., Sweet Potato, Brinjal, Lady’s finger, Cabbage and Tomato. Estimates of average yield and production are arrived at based on the data collected through these experiments.

The key activities of the Improvement of Crop Statistics scheme are the sample check on area enumeration of selected survey/sub-division numbers of the Khasra Register (Adangal) maintained by the Village Administrative Officers and the supervision of Crop Cutting Experiments for some important food crops in State-wide selected sample villages under this scheme.

The purpose of this scheme is to identify deficiencies in the system of collection of Agricultural Statistics in the State by exercising meaningful supervision by the Union and State authorities over the primary field workers viz., the Village Administrative Officers, and to suggest remedial measures for the improvement of the system. The results of this scheme are used by the National Statistical Office (NSO) to effect

The Agriculture Census is a Central Sector Scheme undertaken in Tamil Nadu under the aegis of the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Government of India. The Directorate of Economics and Statistics is the Nodal Directorate for the conduct of the Agriculture Census in Tamil Nadu.

7. Gold carries profound cultural and emotional resonance in Tamil Nadu. Gifting Gold to a newborn celebrates the baby’s arrival, honours the mother’s noble journey and transforms public health delivery into a source of immense community pride. Also, this token remains an enduring asset, generating lasting institutional goodwill that spreads via word of mouth.

8. This culturally meaningful initiative seeks to celebrate motherhood, honour the mother's journey, reinforce confidence in public healthcare services, and strengthen the bond between people and public institutions. The initiative is intended to further strengthen the State's commitment to maternal and child health by promoting equitable access to quality healthcare and ensuring that every mother and new-born receives safe, affordable, and compassionate care through the public health system.

9. The modalities of the Thaimaaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam (&miompesdr She CuonSlnb Hib) are detailed below: -

a. Goals and Objectives

(i) Elevate public healthcare settings from a baseline necessity to a preferred destination of pride and celebration, with dignity at birth.

(ii) | Reclaiming the Government institutional deliveries by offering a high-value, permanent tangible benefit that complements the existing maternity cash benefits and maternal kits.

(iii) | Erase socio-economic bias surrounding public health facility deliveries, recognizing that every mother's journey is noble and every child is a treasure.

b. Target Beneficiaries with Eligible criteria (i) | Resident of Tamil Nadu is eligible for the scheme.
